# On the Peculiar Joy of Being Lost

There's a particular quality to being lost that nobody talks about anymore. We live in an age where being lost is theoretically impossible—you're never more than a few taps away from knowing exactly where you are, what restaurants are nearby, and what the optimal route is to get where you're going. GPS has eliminated one of the last great uncertainties of human experience, and I'm not sure we've fully reckoned with what we've lost in gaining that certainty.

I'm thinking about this because I got lost yesterday in a part of my city I've driven through a hundred times. My phone died—just completely drained battery—and I took a wrong turn somewhere around Fifth and Main, and suddenly I was in a part of the grid I couldn't quite orient myself in. The streets were familiar but arranged in an unfamiliar way. Nothing was where my mental map said it should be.

For about seven minutes, I felt genuinely uncertain. And then something unexpected happened: I felt alive in a way I hadn't in months.

There's a freedom in not knowing where you are. When you can't consult the oracle of your phone, when you can't instantly resolve the question of "where am I?", you have to actually pay attention. You have to look at street signs. You have to notice that you're in a neighborhood that's maybe a little seedier than you expected, with a vintage clothing store you've never seen before, and a man playing saxophone on the corner, and a small park with a fountain that someone has filled with floating flowers. You have to make a choice—do I turn left or right? And that choice, which is trivial in terms of consequences, feels momentous in a way that algorithmic navigation has trained us to forget.

I think we've optimized for efficiency and lost something in the bargain. Not just the pleasant getting-lost, but the fundamental human experience of being uncertain, of having to make decisions without perfect information, of having to live with a little confusion about how the world is arranged.

This connects to something I've been thinking about more broadly—this sense that we've removed friction from nearly every aspect of life, and that the removal of friction has been presented as pure good, when actually some amount of friction is essential to being human.

Consider the act of buying something. Thirty years ago, if you wanted a book, you had to figure out what you wanted, find the store, drive there, hope they had it in stock, talk to someone who might give you a recommendation you didn't ask for, and then pay for it while the cashier asked you personal questions. It was inefficient. Now you type three words and it arrives two days later. This is objectively better in every measurable way. And yet something is missing.

What's missing is the encounter with the unexpected. The possibility that while searching for one thing, you'd find something better. The experience of being a human in a space with other humans, transacting not just money but small moments of connection. The friction—the time spent, the effort required—is part of what gives the transaction meaning.

I've noticed this same thing with how we consume information. We used to have to find knowledge. You'd hear something interesting, not quite understand it, and then you'd have to go to the library and track down books, talk to experts, piece together understanding over weeks or months. Now you type it into Google and have seven equally-valid explanations in thirty seconds. We're drowning in information and starving for meaning, because meaning requires time and effort and the kind of productive struggle that we've successfully engineered out of existence.

The weird thing is that we invented all these friction-removing tools ostensibly to give ourselves more time for what matters. We were supposed to save time on mundane tasks and thereby have more space for creativity, relationships, contemplation. But instead—and I think this is the dark joke of modernity—we've filled all that recovered time with more tasks, more consumption, more stimulation. We're faster than ever and more rushed than ever.

I read somewhere that attention is not actually a renewable resource—that there's a fixed amount of it in human consciousness, and it can't be regenerated by sleep or rest the way energy can. I don't know if that's neurologically true, but it feels true experientially. The more I try to do, the less genuinely present I am for any of it. I'm like a computer with too many tabs open, running more slowly, delivering diminishing returns on every action.

There's a technology writer named Cal Newport who talks about "deep work"—the idea that meaningful work requires extended periods of uninterrupted focus, and that the constant connectivity and stimulation of modern life has made deep work nearly impossible. He's right, I think, but I'd extend it beyond work. Deep living might require the same thing. It might require the capacity to be bored, to be lost, to be confused, to be uncertain.

One of the things that strikes me about children is their capacity for what seems like empty time but is actually quite full. A kid can sit in the grass for an hour just... noticing things. Following an ant. Watching clouds. Bored, by adult standards, but doing something neurologically profound—basically getting to know the world through direct perception rather than through filtered information.

We medicate this capacity out of children now. We call it ADHD. Maybe some of it genuinely is a neurological difference, but I wonder how much of it is that we've simply lowered our tolerance for a certain kind of restless attention. We expect children to engage with pre-designed stimulation, and when they prefer to stare out windows or lose themselves in repetitive play, we interpret that as dysfunction rather than the normal human mode of being.

I'm not being a romantic about the past. Obviously people in earlier eras had profound frustrations with their lack of access to information, with the time costs of doing simple things, with inefficiency in general. I'm not arguing that we should go backwards. But I do think there's something worth questioning about our assumption that more efficiency is automatically better, that more information is automatically better, that friction is always an enemy.

There's a reason that people with access to every streaming service become paradoxed by choice and end up watching nothing. There's a reason that people with unlimited information often know less than they think. There's a reason that people with more labor-saving devices than any humans in history often feel busier. There's a reason that I felt more engaged yesterday, lost in my own city, than I have in weeks of optimized, efficient living.

I've been thinking about this in relation to reading, too. For most of human history, books were hard to come by. If you found a book, you read it carefully. You reread it. You let it work on you over time. Now I have thousands of books available instantly, and I skim them. I read the summary, get the main ideas, move on. It's more efficient—I encounter more ideas—but I'm less changed by any of them. The friction of rarity and scarcity actually made reading more meaningful.

There's something almost liturgical about how people used to engage with knowledge. They'd read the same book multiple times. They'd memorize passages. They'd think about what they'd read for years. The limited supply forced a kind of depth. Now we have an infinite supply and we're spiritually starving.

The weird thing is knowing this and not being able to stop. I have access to infinite information and infinite entertainment, and I can't seem to stop checking it. It's not like the old days, when you could decide not to go to the library. The library is in my pocket, and it's constantly pinging me, constantly offering me new stimulation. The friction is gone and I resent it.

I've been trying an experiment. I'm intentionally introducing friction back into my life. I'm reading physical books and staying with them, even when they're slow. I'm deliberately not looking things up immediately when I'm curious about them—I'm letting the uncertainty sit for a while, letting my mind work on the question. I'm leaving my phone at home sometimes. I'm getting lost on purpose, taking routes I don't know, letting myself be confused about where I am.

It feels kind of stupid, honestly. Like I'm deliberately creating problems that we solved. But it's also the most present I've felt in a long time.

There's a concept in Japanese aesthetics called "ma"—it refers to the empty space in art, the silence in music, the space between things. It's not the absence of something but an essential presence. It's the pause that makes the note meaningful. The blank space that makes the image coherent. Japanese gardens are full of ma—negative space that's actually doing the heavy lifting of making the garden beautiful and meaningful.

I think we've eliminated ma from modern life. We've filled every space, every moment, every second of silence with stimulus. And we're missing the way that emptiness is actually what makes fullness meaningful.

When I was lost yesterday, I was experiencing ma. I was in an uncertain space, and that emptiness—that lack of predetermined path and known destination—made the experience vivid and real in a way that optimized efficiency erases.

I don't have a grand conclusion here. I'm not going to suggest we all smash our phones and move to the woods. I'm not even going to suggest that the friction-removing technologies are bad, exactly. They're not. They're genuinely wonderful for many things. But I think we've been naive about the tradeoffs. We've eliminated friction and been surprised that we've also eliminated meaning.

The challenge now is not to have the technology—we're not going backwards—but to be intentional about when we use it and when we don't. To recognize that some inefficiency is actually efficiency, in the sense that it gets us more of what we actually want. To understand that a certain kind of friction—the productive struggle, the productive boredom, the productive confusion—is part of living a full human life.

Maybe the most subversive thing we can do now is to deliberately get lost. To choose inefficiency sometimes. To let ourselves be uncertain. To sit with not-knowing. To introduce ma back into our lives intentionally, because the world no longer provides it accidentally.

I'm going to kill my phone's location services, at least for a while. I'm going to get lost sometimes on purpose. I'm going to let myself be confused. And I'm going to see if that brings me back to life in some way that pure efficiency never could.

Being lost, it turns out, is a kind of being found.
